title: Providence and the Displacement of Counselors
english: According to the saying, "they shall build and I will turn back," says the Lord (Job 22:28). And concerning those having a bad building, it is said: "you destroy them and will not build them." Thus, if it is shut according to men, no one will open; for if God is not prospering a certain action, which someone pre-ordains, through whom words are known, who is able to open? He shut the escape from Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and an opening was not found. And in its entirety, many such things you will find.

For He closes against the useful, not allowing the enjoyment of human things, but to be in want; and toward what? Toward salvation, He brings the difficult things. And He closes in another way according to men, when He does not allow them to prosper in evils, and this happening properly toward God, not as the Pharisees did; for it was said to them: "you shut the kingdom of the heavens, you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter" (Matt 23:13). And the kingdom of the heavens is shut when those who seem to be teachers, through whom they work evils, make certain imitators of themselves, so that neither they nor those imitating them may enter into the kingdom.

If, therefore, God also shuts to the one who has shut [it] because of his conduct, who will open to him? Likewise the water and that which hinders according to the sensible, according to what is said, "one part shall be shortened and a part, on which I will not wet, shall be dried," hinders, it dries the earth; and of this you have the example in the Kingdoms; for He is "the one raising clouds from the end of the earth, making lightning into rain" (Job 37:3). And according to His own authority, He touches the earth toward growth and toward destruction of those in it, as in the flood according to Noah (Gen 7).

But if you lead these up with understanding, you will find also the profit from them. With Him are power and strength, with Him are knowledge and understanding. The reasonable proof of each of those things happening from Him, the God, is that no one else would be able to do it, or Him, as He teaches, asserting: "with Him are power and strength." And so that no one may irrationally suppose that He makes God remain by power and strength alone, He brings: "with Him are knowledge and understanding." For even if someone is displeased with the things happening, saying, "why is this fertile and wealthy land again becoming a wasteland, while the needy remains without bread?", let him hear.

The phrase 'with him are knowledge and understanding.' For He himself, 'having arranged all things by weight and measure,' provides to each according to the words of His providence what He wills. The production or administration of existing things does not occur by chance, but the diversity of created things and the wisdom of administration have come from and stand in divine wisdom.

It must be noted that it is not said, as if God were a compounder, that 'strength and might are with him' and 'with him are knowledge and understanding'; for all these things the Son is, being simple and uncomposite. He leads away captive counselors, and he makes the judges of the earth err. And these are the works of providence; for by will and by judgment, captive counselors are led away and judges are displaced.

And if 'counselors' refers to those who blow great in the state, many of these are also found scattered in captivity; which is clear from the captivity of Israel, concerning which Jeremiah lamented over their city, saying: 'How sits the city once full of people, now as a widow full of nations; she who ruled among the lands has become a tributary' (Jeremiah 2:36). And if 'those who advise' signifies the name of counsel, then God leads away those who do this for evil. An example of this is Ahithophel, whose counsel and life were perverted.

For from this also one can understand the work of providence: that even those most wise among those advising, following the purpose of advising, fail in their outcomes, not as if they advised badly, but as if providence is testing them otherwise. So also rulers who have done all things by themselves fail; for the end belongs to God. By His own power He 'made judges err.' And if 'made err' signifies madness, this also happens to those using judgment in a way that is not required; for God displaces such people, proving them foolish. But 'made err' can also signify their displacement; for by the providence of the Word of God, 'judges are displaced' and kings are seated on thrones. Similar to this is 'through me kings reign' and 'the Lord establishes kings and removes them.' Often He gives these both in anger and according to...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Scattering of Counsel and the Pouring Out of Dishonor
english: The phrase 'I gave them a kingdom in my wrath' is used. Because things apart from God's judgment are hollow, He himself says, lamenting, 'They reigned and not through me; they began and did not make known to me' (Ps 2:2), through which, in wrath, such people are again released, the opportunity for reconciliation being provided again for a time.

For a throne is often taken to mean a kingdom, even if it is used instead of a teaching office, as is clear from 'The Lord King is established forever' (Ps 145:13), and again: 'Your throne, O God, is unto the ages of ages' (Ps 45:6), and even more: 'A throne of authority is prepared with righteousness' (Ps 89:14). But it is also said to the disciples: 'You also shall sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel' (Matt 19:28). When it is said, 'The scribes sat upon the seat of Moses' (Luke 13:31), this seat is one of teaching. And he girded their loins with a belt. Unless he himself lives, the one being girded has no strength; therefore, it is God who is He and who governs all these things by His own providence. And the matter of the belt signifies as 'And rulers shall hold the earth through me.'

He sends them as captives. If he speaks of those not using the matter correctly, it shows that He spares not even them when the time calls. But if he means those using it according to what is necessary, God also sends even these many times, like those concerning Daniel and Jesus the son of Josadak, into captivity for the sake of the usefulness of another multitude; for how great was the thing they were doing, they were not worthy to undergo captivity. Consider, however, the greatness of them, that even having become captives and being in Babylon, they remained unshaken.

And if, then, we see the saints being sent into this life, let us reckon that it was not for their own sake, but they underwent this for the benefit of others. The apostle, alluding to this, writes: 'This attitude was among you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, did not consider being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave' (Phil 2:6-7). He destroyed the powerful ones of the earth. For it is by the judgment of this God that these also undergo destruction, just as Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar. And God destroyed the arch-evil devil; for it is said: 'But the angels who do not obey...'

He scatters the lips of the faithful. Some think that certain words are faithful and unanswerable, and God scatters these. Without fail, it is said concerning Ahithophel, the counselor of King Israel, who was previously a counselor to David and later to Absalom; for it was said of him that the counsel of Ahithophel was like the counsel of God, and this was being circulated about him as being unsearchable in his counsels. Without fail, David, to whom the unmanifest and the hidden things of wisdom were revealed, praying to God said, 'Scatter the counsel of Ahithophel' (2 Sam 15:31), and so it happened. He recognized the understanding of the elders.

And he recognized the understanding of the elders who have instead of many [opinions] prudence and the unceasing life instead of old age; for it was worthy of his knowledge. It is appropriate to hear 'recognized' in the sense of understanding; for he also recognizes the foolish and their counsels. But it is clear how he, recognizing those things—speaking of the elders according to Abraham—accepts them. Pouring out dishonor upon rulers, but humbling the lowly. For of him who 'appoints and removes' (1 Sam 2:7), it means to grant honors in the appointing, and to pour out dishonor in the removing; and to 'pour out' signifies doing this abundantly; for many times we have observed this, as in 'the love of God is poured out in our hearts' (Rom 5:5), instead of 'has been greatly given' according to what is said; 'a myrrh emptied out [is] your name,' which became 'a wonder in all the earth' (Ps 72:15) according to the Psalmist, before this sending out the fragrance only to Judah, and later reaching all, as it is said, 'You have magnified your holy name over all.' But it also serves as a demonstration of the grace being abundantly given, 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28). Therefore he says that there will be a pouring out of dishonor upon rulers according to justice, of those being humbled by God; for he himself makes the honored dishonorable, the poor rich, and the weak strong, according to him who 'raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the ash heap' (1 Sam 2:8). But if you take the lowly according to opinion and choice, he humbled them by 'making [them] into highness.'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Shadow of Death and Divine Wandering
english: He prevents a perceived destruction by making things appear insignificant, according to the principle of 'treating non-existent things as if they were existing.' Thus he says: 'Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you in due time' (1 Peter 5:6). And again: 'The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble' (James 4:6). For he brings those who have perfected the virtue of humility into the kingdom of heaven; for he is the one about whom it is said: 'And he will save the poor in spirit' (Matthew 5:3). He reveals deep things out of darkness.

Having said this, he will proceed regarding creation and providence, and regarding foreknowledge and his unchangeable nature, as well as knowing the things being done in secret. Similar to this is what is said by David: 'Lord, you have tested me and known me; you knew my seat and my rising; you understood all my thoughts from afar' (Psalm 139:2). For it is not that when I reason, you come to know my thoughts, but rather you exist as a foreknower of things, and so also of thoughts. 'Where shall I go from your spirit, or from your face where shall I flee? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I descend to Hades, you are there; if I take up the wings of my dawn and dwell at the limits of the sea, even there your hand will guide and your right hand will hold me fast' (Psalm 139:7-10).

But even beyond these things, he says something else in the 'I said: therefore darkness shall overpower me,' instead of 'hide me.' But even this, teaching again that the knowledge of God cannot be prevented, he says: 'The darkness shall not be darkness from you, and night shall be enlightened as the day' (Psalm 18:11). For to men, indeed, the night makes a difference from the day, but to you, O Lord, even these things are enlightened, instead of 'they become manifest'; which is also what the apostle makes manifest, saying: 'all things are naked and laid bare to the eyes of him' (Hebrews 4:13). And in Daniel it is said: 'knowing all things in the darkness, and the light is with him' (Daniel 2:22), which is our Savior, who 'enlightens every man' (John 1:9). Therefore, everything is manifest to him... and the deeds of men, those happening in secret and in darkness, he makes manifest when it is necessary. And he is also able to reveal the obscure parts of words, according to 'he will understand a parable and a dark saying' (Matthew 13:35), through enlightenment.

Having become mine in thought, he led the shadow of death into light. Now he calls the shadow of death the wickedness which is hidden and operating with deceit toward someone, as if to call the shadow of death himself. For often those operating are signified by the name of the virtue, just as the righteous is called righteousness in 'that we might become the righteousness of God in Him' (2 Cor 5:21). And the apostle, regarding those having love, indicated it by the name of love, saying: 'Love is patient, does not boast, is not rude, does not think of evil, believes all things' (1 Cor 13:4). He does not speak these things concerning the virtue, but concerning the one having the love.

Then again he selects: 'Love never fails' (1 Cor 13:8); and it is not a great thing that a virtue 'does not fail'—it is not its nature—but he speaks concerning the one established in this; for as much as anyone has of it, he is not to be lost. Therefore, if he says 'to lead the shadow of death into light', he does not mean the wickedness, but he speaks of the one operating it, according to 'for you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord' (Eph 5:8). For when they were darkness, existing in ignorance, they happened to be a shadow of death. But when he enlightened them having known them, then he led them out from the shadow of death, so that it might be said concerning them: 'as luminaries in the world' (Phil 2:15), who 'having put away the lie', which is 'darkness', 'speak the truth', which is what is light.

He is wandering nations and destroying them. Wandering is a homonym. For deception is also called wandering, and lawlessness is called wandering, according to that which is said: 'and they became wanderers among the nations' (Acts 13:41). But God does not wander in an unwholesome way in doing this, but is pulling them away from wickedness. And if he also says that 'to deliver to a reprobate mind' is wandering (2 Thess 2:11), he does not do this in an unwholesome way, as it is heard from the Lord saying: 'Behold, I will send him a delusion' (2 Thess 2:11), which is: because he turns toward evils, while caring for his salvation, God turns him away, instead of the soul prospering in evils. He turns him toward a useful wandering placed for him. In the same manner, it is said that he destroys the wicked, either by subjecting them to punishment or by destroying their vice through a turning back. Thus, God either destroys the nations by punishing them or by destroying their wickedness. So also 'to seek and...
